Hi. This is Agent Office, my entry for the AWS Agents for Humans hackathon. It is a personal agent tribe that lives in a pixel office: Strands Agents running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with a face you can actually watch work.

The idea is simple. A serious harness for personal agents, wrapped in the fun of a game. You build the team: name an agent, say what it does, give it a computer and the account passes it needs. The agents live in a room. Each has a desk. They walk to the letterbox for mail and to the wall calendar for the diary, and they only sit at the keyboard when they are really using a computer. Underneath it is a real harness: identity, chat memory, unattended jobs, approvals, budgets and evals. And it is built on AWS end to end.

Here is the architecture. You reach it from the browser or from Telegram. App Runner hosts the UI server, which handles Cognito sign in, signs requests to the runtime, receives the Telegram webhook and edits routines. The agents themselves run in Bedrock AgentCore Runtime, using the Strands TypeScript SDK in an arm 64 container. Models come from Amazon Bedrock: Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus. AgentCore Identity holds the OAuth tokens for Gmail and Google Calendar. AgentCore Code Interpreter and Browser give each agent a sandboxed VM and a real browser. DynamoDB and S3 keep the state, and EventBridge Scheduler is the clock for routines, invoking the runtime directly with no Lambda in between.

In the room you watch the work happen. Thought clouds show the model reasoning. Pictograms show which tool is running. The monitor lights up only for real computer use, a shell, a file, or the browser, and then it shows the live page. Mail is a walk to the letterbox. The diary is a walk to the wall calendar. Click an agent to see its card: mood, tasks, tools and passes. The green plumbob is a nod to the game that inspired all this.

The Foundry is where you build your tribe. Up to four agents. Slot one is the boss you talk to, the rest are colleagues it delegates to. The computer you give an agent decides its brain. A salvaged terminal runs Haiku with no hardware. An office workstation runs Sonnet with a sandbox and a browser. An overclocked rig runs Opus. Templates come with skills: researcher, writer, scheduler, analyst, operator, each with a playbook that rides in the prompt. And access passes are per agent. No pass, no tools.

You can also dress them like a game character. Skin, hair, hats, glasses, tops, bottoms, shoes, every colour. The same look is drawn seated at the desk, walking the room, and in the portrait card. Hair sways, eyes blink, idle agents stretch and sip coffee. Small things that make a team feel alive.

Identity. Sign in is Amazon Cognito's hosted UI. The server trusts the id token only; nothing the browser sends can change who you are. Your agents, chats and memory follow you to any browser. Telegram becomes the same account with one link code. And AgentCore Identity keeps the Google tokens: the agent asks for consent once, the vault holds the refresh token, and calendar and mail reuse the same provider with different scopes.

Connectors come with guard rails. Real Gmail through the AgentCore token vault, with a stub inbox that works the same way so the whole flow demos offline. Drafts only, never send: the agent prepares, the human sends. Calendar can read and write, but there is no delete tool, because cancelling emails everyone. Nobody gets an invitation unless the user asked for it. Passes are per agent. And link an account and its fixture appears in the room.

Autonomy. Agents that act when not spoken to. Jobs run unattended, started from the browser or by a routine, and every job is also a chat with its full transcript. Routines run on EventBridge Scheduler: weekdays at eight, or every thirty minutes. Each one is a real schedule that invokes the AgentCore runtime directly. Mail and calendar triggers poll cheaply and only wake the model when there is something new. Results and files land on Telegram, or wait in the jobs tab.

But nothing changes your world without a nod. In an unattended run, booking an event or leaving a draft pauses the agent with a Strands interrupt. The paused state, tool call included, is snapshotted by the SDK session manager into S3. Telegram asks you to approve or deny. On approve, the very same tool call completes. On deny, the agent finishes without it and tells you so.

Reliability rails on every agent. A summarising conversation manager so long chats survive. Retries with backoff for throttles, including the pre-stream throttle the default strategy misses. A deadline on every tool. Metering: the SDK's metrics are summed per user per day into DynamoDB, a token budget stops runaway routines, and the energy bar in the room is that real number. Chat history is the SDK's own session snapshots in S3. And twenty scripted evals, all passing.

The tribe. Colleagues used to start every job with an empty head. Now the boss hands over an envelope: a brief, the context it has, the deliverable and constraints, plus who the user is and the house rules. Independent subtasks go out in one turn and run in parallel, and the room animates every busy colleague. Roles come with skills, and there are four desks.

To sum up the AWS services carrying the weight: Amazon Bedrock for the models, AgentCore Runtime for the agents, AgentCore Identity for OAuth, AgentCore Code Interpreter and Browser for hands, Cognito, App Runner and ECR for the front door, and DynamoDB, S3, EventBridge Scheduler and CloudWatch for state, files, time and the logs that explained every bug.
That is Agent Office. Open source under MIT, on GitHub at yashsharma999 slash agent-office. Build a team, give them computers, and watch them work. Thank you.
